> **What this case shows** — washing (ICF **d510**, washing oneself) is the
> self-care task the sibling case (`adl-selfcare-hmp`) had *no data* for. HTAD is
> the one public wrist-accelerometer dataset that labels **washing hands**. Under
> a strict leave-one-subject-out test, the ecosystem's activity-recognition
> pipeline recognises washing at **0.53 recall** — about **3.7×** the **0.14**
> chance level — in a seven-task home-activity problem, cross-subject. **What
> reproduces, and what doesn't** — washing carries a wrist-detectable signature
> above chance; but this rests on **only 3 subjects**, so it is a *demonstration*,
> not a definitive validation, and washing stays confusable with the other
> hand-based tasks. ICF d510 also covers bathing/showering, which HTAD does not
> contain — only hand-washing is tested. **How to read it** — each bar is one
> task's cross-subject recall (red = washing, dashed = 0.14 chance).

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — the same four moves as any wearable ADL recogniser: **window** →
**features** → **classify** → **map to ICF** — applied to the hardest self-care
task to find data for.
**Way of thinking** — when the only public evidence is small (N = 3), say so
*in the result*: run the strict protocol (leave-one-subject-out), report the
above-chance signal, and record the weak evidence wherever the claim propagates
(here, the coverage registry carries `HTAD N=3, recall 0.53`). A small-N
above-chance result is worth publishing *as* small-N.
**Ecosystem usage** — `adlFeatures()` → `trainADL()` / `recognizeADL()` →
`adlToICF()` (PhysioWearable), unchanged from the sibling cases.
:::

## Proposition

On the one public wrist-accelerometer dataset that labels washing hands, the HAR
pipeline recognises washing (ICF d510) at **0.53 recall** under
leave-one-subject-out — about **3.7×** the **0.14** chance level of a seven-task
problem — with a 5-of-7 overall accuracy of **0.63**. This is a small-N
(3-subject) demonstration, honestly not a definitive validation.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from a gap.** The sibling self-care case (HMP) had no
washing data, so d510 stayed *supported* (pipeline-ready, unvalidated). HTAD
(Garcia-Ceja et al. 2021) was built to test *home-task recognition from a wrist
accelerometer and audio*, and — unusually — it includes **washing hands**. We ask
the narrow question the data can answer: does washing carry a wrist-detectable
signature that a recogniser can pick out, across people?

## Challenge & approach

Two challenges: washing hands is a hand-based rubbing motion easily confused with
brushing teeth or eating, and there are only three subjects. We do not hide
either. We window the wrist acceleration, extract the standard 36-feature
descriptor, train a k-nearest-neighbours classifier, and test **leave-one-subject-out**
— train on two people, test on the third, rotate. `adlToICF()` maps washing to
ICF d510.

## Data

The **HTAD** wrist-accelerometer home-task dataset (Garcia-Ceja et al. 2021,
figshare 6667532) — ~31 Hz, 3 subjects, seven home tasks. The exact activities
used are in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Cross-subject recall per home task under leave-one-subject-out; washing (red)
clears the 0.14 chance line (dashed).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* washing sits at **0.53**, well above the seven-task chance
line — a real above-chance signal — while some tasks (watching TV, typing) are
easier and others (grooming) harder. The whole picture rests on three subjects,
so read the *direction* (washing is detectable), not a precise number.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| washing (d510) recall (leave-one-subject-out) | **0.53** |
| chance level (1 / 7 tasks) | 0.14 |
| ratio to chance | ~3.7× |
| 7-task accuracy | 0.63 |
| **subjects** | **3** |

## Conclusion

Washing hands leaves a wrist-detectable signature — a recogniser finds it well
above chance — so ICF d510 can move from *pipeline-ready* to *validated*, with
the honest caveat that this rests on three subjects and covers hand-washing, not
bathing. The transferable takeaway: **a small-N above-chance result is a genuine
result if you report it as small-N and carry the caveat wherever the claim
travels.**

## Open questions

- Three subjects is too few for a definitive washing validation; a larger
  labelled wrist-IMU set with bathing/hand-washing would confirm it, and no
  public wrist dataset yet labels dressing (d540) or toileting (d530).
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

The recipe is identical to the sibling wearable cases:

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| window + extract HAR features | `adlFeatures()` | PhysioWearable |
| train / apply an activity recogniser | `trainADL()` / `recognizeADL()` | PhysioWearable |
| map activities to ICF performance codes | `adlToICF()` | PhysioWearable |

**Choosing the parameters:** with small N, use the strictest split you can
(leave-one-subject-out), report the ratio to chance rather than raw accuracy, and
propagate the sample size into every downstream claim. See `adl-selfcare-hmp` for
the same pipeline at larger N, and `adl-rasch-verbagg` for the capacity side.

```r
library(PhysioWearable)
feats <- adlFeatures(accel, sampling_rate = 31)
model <- trainADL(train_feats, train_labels)
recog <- recognizeADL(model, accel, sampling_rate = 31)
adlToICF(recog)                                     # washing -> d510
```

One line for the technical reader: every number traces to
[`artifacts/summary.csv`](artifacts/summary.csv) and
[`artifacts/per_class_recall.csv`](artifacts/per_class_recall.csv), re-checked by
[`audit.py`](audit.py) and `tools/validate_case.py`.
